title: Concrete Formwork
examWeight: Represents 16% of the Red Seal Carpenter exam, focusing on heavy civil and structural forming

nbcPart9References.title: Footing Dimensions and Step Footings
rules: Footing size is determined by the load-bearing capacity of the soil. Standard footings for stable soil must be at least 100 mm thick, or equal to the projection of the footing beyond the wall, whichever is greater.
Step footing rules (NBC 9.15.3.9): The vertical rise of any step must not exceed 600 mm (24 inches), and the horizontal distance between steps (the run) must be at least 600 mm.
For step footings, the concrete footing must run continuously. Step transitions must be poured monolithically or linked with rebar doweled at least 300 mm (12 inches) into both sections.
Footing projections: The projection of the footing on each side of the foundation wall must be at least 100 mm and must not exceed the thickness of the footing unless reinforced.

nbcPart9References.title: Concrete Testing, Slump, and Placement Standards
rules: The slump test measures the consistency and workability of fresh concrete. A standard slump cone is 300 mm (12 in) high, 200 mm wide at the base, and 100 mm wide at the top, filled in 3 equal volume layers with 25 rod strokes per layer using a 16 mm bullet-nosed rod.
Acceptable slump limits for structural foundation walls are typically between 50 mm and 100 mm, unless superplasticizers (water-reducing admixtures) are added.
Rebar clearance (CSA A23.1): Rebar must have at least 75 mm (3 inches) of concrete cover when poured against and permanently exposed to earth, and 40 mm to 50 mm when exposed to weather.
Splice overlaps: Rebar lap splices must be at least 24 to 40 times the bar diameter (typically 450 mm to 600 mm minimum for 10M (#3) or 15M (#5) bars) to properly transfer tension stresses.

nbcPart9References.title: Wall Form Lateral Pressure Dynamics
rules: Lateral concrete pressure on vertical wall forms behaves as a fluid until set. Pressure is calculated using formula: P = w * h, where w is concrete density (typically 2400 kg/m³ or 150 lb/ft³) and h is fluid head.

Factors increasing lateral pressure: high rate of pour (vertical meters per hour), lower concrete temperatures (which retards curing/chemical setting), mechanical vibration, and use of retarding admixtures.

Form ties must be selected and spaced based on calculated lateral pressure. Standard snap-ties are rated for 3,000 lbs safe working load, while heavy-duty loop ties or taper ties can exceed 5,000 to 15,000 lbs.
Formwork must be braced horizontally to resist wind loads and aligned vertically to ensure plumbness (maximum plumb tolerance is 6 mm over 3 m of height).

nbcPart9References.title: Insulated Concrete Forms (ICF) & Bracing
rules: ICF systems use interlocking expanded polystyrene (EPS) blocks as formwork that remains in place as permanent thermal insulation.
ICF concrete core must be poured in continuous lifts of not more than 1.2 meters (4 feet) per hour to prevent bottom blowouts and alignment bowing.
Alignment bracing with integrated turnbuckles must be installed every 1.5 to 1.8 meters (5 to 6 feet) along the wall perimeter to plumb the walls before and during the pour.

Internal concrete consolidation: ICF walls require careful internal vibration (using a small pencil vibrator, maximum 25 mm diameter head) to prevent honeycombing around rebar without tearing the EPS webbing.

nbcPart9References.title: Concrete Stair Construction & Support
rules: Under NBC 9.8.4, concrete stairs require consistent rise and run. Maximum rise is 200 mm, minimum run is 210 mm, and tread depth must be between 235 mm and 355 mm.
Stair soffit forms (throat thickness) must be at least 100 mm (4 inches) thick at the thinnest point (where the tread and riser intersect the underside angle) to provide structural shear resistance.
Riser boards must be cut with a bottom bevel (or beveled inward) to allow finishing trowels to easily access the entire back edge of the tread below during the pour.
Rebar mats in concrete stairs must sit in the lower third of the slab depth (tension zone) and tie directly into structural landing beams or foundation walls.

footingsAndSteps.title: Step Footings & Base Dimensions
footingsAndSteps.details: When building on sloped terrain, step footings must be used to keep foundations below frost lines while limiting excavation. NBC 9.15.3.9 requires step dimensions to maintain a maximum rise of 600 mm and a minimum run of 600 mm. For steep slopes, multiple smaller steps are structurally superior to a single tall step. The concrete must run continuously; if poured in separate stages, vertical cold-joint bulkheads must be keyed and reinforced with steel dowels. Main footings must be wide enough to support building dead and live loads; on standard soils, 2x4 lumber is used for 100 mm thick residential footing forms.

slumpAndClearance.title: Slump Tests & Rebar Cover Rules
slumpAndClearance.details: The slump test is the primary on-site measure of concrete consistency. A slump too high indicates excess water, which dilutes the cement paste and dramatically reduces concrete compressive strength. Concrete reinforcement relies on chemical bonding and physical rib anchorage. To protect steel rebar from moisture, oxygen, and corrosive salts (which cause spalling and failure), strict cover rules are enforced: 75 mm of concrete must surround rebar in contact with soil, 40 mm for weather-exposed concrete, and 20 mm for interior elements. Lap splices must overlap sufficiently to transfer structural tension.

wallPressures.title: Wall Pressures & Formwork Failures
wallPressures.details: Formwork is a temporary structure designed to contain heavy fluid concrete. Liquid concrete exerts hydrostatic pressure that increases with depth. If the rate of pour is too fast, or the temperature is cold, concrete remains liquid for longer, piling up weight at the base of the forms. If form ties are spaced too far, or if there are missing waler brackets, forms will bow or catastrophically rupture (blow out). Standard plyform (wood) and steel-framed panel systems must be tied with snap ties or taper ties, backed by horizontal double-walers and vertical strongbacks to keep alignment perfectly straight.

icfSystems.title: ICF Engineering & Pour Control
icfSystems.details: ICF structures provide excellent energy efficiency but require specialized pouring techniques. Unlike heavy wood forms, lightweight EPS blocks can float, lift, or drift if poured too fast. Concreting must occur in continuous horizontal circles (lifts) of 1.0 to 1.2 meters high per hour. Turnbuckle bracing systems are anchored to the ground to keep walls vertical. Carpenters must ensure window and door openings (bucks) are heavily braced internally to resist the inward crush of concrete, and that horizontal rebar is slotted securely into the form webbing.

concreteStairs.title: Concrete Stair Layout & Forming Mechanics
concreteStairs.details: Concrete stairs are heavy structural slabs that require robust forming. The stair soffit forms the ramp of the staircase, built using 3/4" plywood sheathing supported by joists and heavy adjustable shores. Riser forms must span between side stringers and be braced with a vertical runner down the center of the stairs to prevent the outward bowing of wet concrete. Throat thickness (the structural concrete depth below the inner step angle) must be a minimum of 100 mm (4 in) and reinforced with a double-directional rebar grid. Riser boards should have beveled bottom edges to let finishers work the concrete flat.

questions.question: A carpenter is calculating the volume of concrete required to pour a continuous footing for a commercial building. The footing is exactly 48.00 meters long, 600 mm wide, and 300 mm deep. How many cubic meters of concrete are required? (Include a standard 10% waste allowance in your final total).
questions.explanation:
1. Find the base volume: Volume = Length * Width * Depth.
Width = 600 mm = 0.60 m. Depth = 300 mm = 0.30 m.
Volume = 48.00 m * 0.60 m * 0.30 m = 8.64 m³.
2. Add the 10% waste factor: Total Volume = 8.64 m³ * 1.10 = 9.504 cubic meters (rounded to 9.50 m³).

questions.question: A concrete wall form is 2.4 meters high, 12.0 meters long, and 200 mm thick. If the concrete is poured at a rate of 1.2 vertical meters per hour at a temperature of 21°C, and the design specifies 15M (#5) vertical rebar spaced at 400 mm o.c., what is the total volume of concrete required to fill the wall, excluding waste?
questions.explanation:
To calculate the concrete volume of the wall:
Volume = Height * Length * Thickness.
Height = 2.4 m, Length = 12.0 m, Thickness = 200 mm = 0.20 m.
Volume = 2.4 * 12.0 * 0.20 = 5.76 cubic meters.

questions.question: A step footing must traverse a slope. The vertical height change is 2.4 meters. Under NBC 9.15.3.9, if the carpenter uses the maximum allowable vertical rise for each step to minimize the number of steps, how many steps are required, and what is the minimum cumulative horizontal length (run) of these step footings?
questions.explanation:
1. Under NBC 9.15.3.9, the maximum vertical rise per step is 600 mm (0.60 m).
Number of steps = Total Rise / Max Step Rise = 2.4 m / 0.60 m = 4 steps.
2. NBC 9.15.3.9 also mandates that the minimum horizontal run of each step footing must be 600 mm (0.60 m).
Minimum cumulative run = Number of steps * Min Step Run = 4 * 0.60 m = 2.4 meters.

questions.question: A rectangular concrete slab on grade measures 15.00 meters wide by 24.00 meters long, with a designed thickness of 125 mm. How many cubic yards of concrete must be ordered to pour this slab, assuming a 5% waste factor? (Note: 1 cubic meter = 1.30795 cubic yards).
questions.explanation:
1. Calculate volume in cubic meters: 
Volume = 15.00 m * 24.00 m * 0.125 m = 45.00 m³.
2. Add 5% waste: 45.00 * 1.05 = 47.25 m³.
3. Convert to cubic yards: 47.25 m³ * 1.30795 = 61.8 cubic yards. (Without waste, it would be 58.9 yd³). Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.question: Under CSA A23.1, a carpenter is setting up formwork for a structural bridge pier that will be poured directly against the earth excavation face. What is the minimum concrete cover (clearance) required between the reinforcing steel (rebar) and the outside face of the concrete?
questions.explanation: Under CSA A23.1 and building codes, concrete poured directly against and permanently exposed to earth requires a minimum rebar cover of 75 mm (3 inches) to protect the steel from moisture and soil chemicals which cause rapid corrosion and structural breakdown.

questions.question: A concrete column form is 450 mm in diameter and 4.2 meters high. What is the precise volume of concrete needed to pour three identical columns? (Use the circle area formula, and exclude waste).
questions.explanation:
1. Find area of the column cross section: Area = Pi * r².
Diameter = 450 mm = 0.45 m, Radius = 0.225 m.
Area = 3.14159 * (0.225)² = 3.14159 * 0.050625 ≈ 0.15904 m².
2. Volume of one column = Area * Height = 0.15904 * 4.2 ≈ 0.668 m³.
3. Total volume for 3 columns = 0.668 * 3 ≈ 2.004 cubic meters.

questions.question: While performing a slump test on a fresh batch of structural concrete, the cone is removed and the concrete slumps vertically by 140 mm. How should the carpenter classify this slump, and what is its structural implication?
options: Low slump; indicating extremely dry, hard-to-work concrete.
Medium slump; ideal for high-plumb structural walls with dense rebar.
High slump; indicating excess water and potential reduction in final compressive strength.
Shear slump; indicating the test must be discarded and repeated.
questions.explanation: A vertical drop of 140 mm (approx 5.5 inches) represents a High Slump. High slump concrete flows easily but, unless achieved using specialized plasticizing admixtures, indicates that too much water was added to the concrete mix on-site. Excess water dilutes the cement paste, creates internal microscopic voids, and drastically reduces the final concrete compressive strength (MPa rating).

questions.question: A carpenter is constructing formwork for a set of concrete steps. To ensure the steps have sufficient structural shear strength, the 'throat thickness' (the minimum diagonal concrete thickness of the stairs) must be formed to which minimum dimension?
questions.explanation: For cast-in-place concrete stairs, the structural slab thickness (known as the throat thickness) is measured diagonally from the inside corner of the step treads to the soffit. Standard trade practice and structural engineering codes require a minimum throat thickness of 100 mm (4 inches) to resist shear forces and bending moments under load.

questions.question: A concrete wall form is being designed for a high-volume pour. The concrete density is 2400 kg/m³. If the concrete is poured rapidly to a liquid height of 3.0 meters before setting begins, what is the hydrostatic lateral pressure exerted at the bottom-most point of the vertical wall form?
questions.explanation:
Hydrostatic pressure is calculated as: P = density * gravity * height.
Density = 2400 kg/m³, Gravity ≈ 9.81 m/s², Height = 3.0 m.
P = 2400 * 9.81 * 3.0 = 70,632 Pascals = 70.63 kPa.
This massive lateral force requires heavy-duty form ties, wales, and strongbacks to prevent form blowout.

questions.question: When pouring concrete into Insulated Concrete Forms (ICF), NBC 9.15.4 mandates strict control over the pour rate and method. What is the maximum recommended height for a single concrete lift to prevent form blowout and core compression?
questions.explanation: To prevent excessive hydrostatic pressures from compressing or bursting the lightweight expanded polystyrene (EPS) blocks, ICF walls must be poured in controlled lifts (layers) of not more than 1.2 meters (4 feet) in height per hour. The concrete must be vibrated gently using a pencil vibrator to eliminate voids.

questions.question: A structural slab requires 20M (#6) reinforcing bars to be lap-spliced (overlapped) to transmit structural loads. If the structural notes specify a minimum lap splice length of 30 times the bar diameter (30d), what is the required overlap length for 20M (#6) bars? (Note: A 20M (#6) bar has a nominal diameter of 20 mm).
questions.explanation:
Lap splice length = 30 * Bar Diameter.
For a 20M (#6) bar (20 mm diameter):
Splice Length = 30 * 20 mm = 600 mm.

questions.question: During concrete placement on a cold autumn day (5°C), how does temperature affect the lateral pressure exerted on vertical wall forms compared to a warm summer pour (25°C)?
options: Cold temperatures decrease lateral pressure because concrete freezes instantly.
Cold temperatures increase lateral pressure because they retard concrete setting times, meaning concrete remains fluid for a longer vertical duration.
Temperature has no effect on form pressures; only height determines pressure.
Cold temperatures decrease pressure because chemical hydration is accelerated.
questions.explanation: Cold temperatures retard the chemical hydration of cement, slowing down concrete's setting time. Because concrete remains liquid (fluid) for a longer period, a rapid pour will build up a larger 'fluid head' (liquid depth), which dramatically increases the lateral hydrostatic pressure at the base of vertical forms, requiring stronger tying and bracing.

questions.question: A carpenter is constructing vertical concrete column forms. To prevent concrete from separating (segregation) as it is poured from the mixer truck, what is the maximum vertical drop distance allowed for concrete before a tremie chute or elephant trunk must be utilized?
questions.explanation: Under concrete placement codes (CSA A23.1), fresh concrete must not be allowed to free-fall more than 1.5 meters (5 feet). Drops exceeding this height cause segregation, where heavy aggregate falls to the bottom first, separating from the water and cement paste, which results in weak, honeycombed concrete.

questions.question: A commercial concrete foundation is designed with a continuous keyway on top of the footing. What is the structural purpose of this keyway, and how is it typically formed?
options: To allow drainage water to pass; formed using 1/2" weeping pipe.
To provide lateral shear resistance between the footing and the wall; formed by depressing a beveled 2x4 lumber key into the wet concrete footing.
To accommodate horizontal rebar; formed using plastic electrical conduit.
To prevent frost penetration; formed by spraying retarders on the concrete surface.
questions.explanation: A keyway is a longitudinal slot cast into the top center of a footing. Its purpose is to lock the subsequent foundation wall to the footing, providing mechanical shear resistance against lateral soil pressures pushing on the wall. It is formed by pressing a beveled 2x4 wood strip into the top of the freshly poured footing and removing it once the concrete has stiffened.

questions.question: A carpenter must pour a concrete retaining wall that is 1.8 meters high. To keep the formwork perfectly straight and prevent alignment bowing, horizontal 'double-walers' are installed across the panel forms. What is the structural purpose of using double-walers instead of single lumber walers?
options: To double the thickness of wood forms.
To allow snap-ties to pass directly between the two lumber members without drilling holes, while distributing pressure horizontally.
To prevent moisture from warping the outer plyform panels.
questions.explanation: Double-walers consist of two parallel pieces of lumber (typically 2x4s) clamped horizontally against vertical form studs. Using two spaced members allows the steel rods of snap-ties to pass directly through the gap between them, eliminating the need to drill holes through structural walers, while evenly transferring the massive lateral concrete loads to the snap-tie washers.

questions.question: Concrete forms for suspended slabs or beams must remain supported by adjustable structural shores until the concrete has cured sufficiently. Under CSA A23.1, what is the minimum typical compressive strength the concrete must achieve before structural shores can be safely removed?
options: 20 MPa (~3000 PSI) or 75% of design strength
questions.explanation: Under CSA A23.1, formwork and shoring for suspended structural elements must remain in place until the concrete has achieved a minimum compressive strength of 20 MPa (~3000 PSI), or at least 75% of its specified 28-day design strength (whichever is greater), as verified by cylinder compression tests.

questions.question: A carpenter is building formwork for a concrete beam. Under structural loads, where does the maximum tension occur in a simple-span beam, and where should the primary longitudinal reinforcing steel be positioned?
options: At the neutral axis in the exact center.
In the upper third of the beam depth.
In the lower third of the beam depth (bottom zone).
At the extreme vertical outer edges of the formwork.
questions.explanation: Concrete is extremely strong in compression but very weak in tension. In a simple-span beam supported at both ends, vertical loads cause the beam to bend downward. This creates compressive stress in the top half of the beam and tension (stretching) stress in the bottom half. Therefore, the primary longitudinal rebar must be positioned in the bottom third of the beam (tension zone) to prevent structural failure.

questions.question: A carpenter is pouring a 3.0 m high wall form. During mechanical internal vibration to consolidate concrete, how should the pencil vibrator be inserted and manipulated to prevent structural voids (honeycombing) and cold joints?
options: Vibrate horizontally by dragging the head along the top surface.
Insert vertically, letting the head penetrate 100-150 mm into the previously poured lift, holding for 5-15 seconds, and extracting slowly.
Hold the vibrator against the exterior form plywood to rattle the panels.
Keep the vibrator continuously running inside the concrete, moving it rapidly back and forth.
questions.explanation: To consolidate concrete properly and merge adjacent lifts without cold joints, the pencil vibrator must be inserted vertically. The head must penetrate 100 to 150 mm (4 to 6 inches) into the underlying lift to fuse the concrete layers. The operator must hold it steady for 5 to 15 seconds until air bubbles stop rising, then withdraw it slowly to allow the concrete paste to fill the void behind the probe.

questions.question: A carpenter is constructing concrete stair forms against a structural concrete wall. To ensure that the stair treads can be finished flat and level, how should the wooden riser boards be cut?
options: Cut with a bottom bevel of 15 to 30 degrees to allow trowels to reach the back of the tread below.
Cut with a 45-degree vertical miter across the face.
Reversed and padded with closed-cell foam tape.
questions.explanation: Riser boards should be cut with a bottom bevel (beveled inward toward the step). This bevel creates a clear pocket of space at the bottom of the board, allowing concrete finishers to float and trowel the back of the underlying tread completely flat without hitting the bottom edge of the riser board with their steel tools.

questions.question: A commercial structural wall requires 15M (#5) rebar tied into a double horizontal grid. If a carpenter is preparing wire ties, what is the most common wire gauge and tie type used to secure overlapping intersections to prevent shifting during concrete vibration?
options: 16-gauge (or 18-gauge) annealed steel wire, double-strand snap tie (or saddle tie)
questions.explanation: The standard rebar tying material is 16-gauge or 18-gauge black annealed steel wire. Annealed wire is flexible enough to twist tightly without breaking. A simple snap tie (single tie) or a saddle tie is used at intersections, tightened with rebar pliers, to ensure the reinforcing cage remains perfectly rigid under concrete flow and heavy internal vibrators.
